Life With Ferris: The Truth About Hydrangeas

  • Monday, November 2, 2026
  • Ferris Robinson
Ruby Slippers
Total Eclipse
Haas Halo
Alice
Ferris Robinson
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:56
Instaread

Mary Leland Davenport refers to an acclaimed entomologist, bestselling “New York Times” author, ecologist, conservationist and college professor as, “My man, Doug Tallamy”.

This recipient of the National Wildlife Federation’s Conservation Leadership Award and the George Robert White Medal of Honor would be thrilled with this moniker. He’s just that sort of guy. Not judgy at all, he has sparked a national movement to turn private yards into thriving conservation corridors.

When we plant with Dr. Tallamy’s (also a doctor) vision in mind, November becomes the absolute sweet spot for adding hardy shrubs to our mountain landscapes. The intense summer heat is finally behind us, but the soil stays warm well into autumn. A shrub planted now doesn’t waste energy keeping soft leaves alive under a baking July sun. Instead, it spends all autumn and winter quietly growing a massive, resilient root system. By spring, it is ready to take off.

If you are looking to add a shrub this month, hydrangeas are likely at the top of your list. They are a staple of southern gardens, but they also hide a massive botanical secret. Depending on the variety you buy, a hydrangea can either be a vital lifeline for local wildlife or an absolute ecological desert.

We all know the mophead hydrangeas are almost entirely sterile, meaning zero pollen or nectar for bees. The Annabelle, Incrediball, Nikko Blue, Limelight, Gatsby Moon … yep. Useless. We whine, “But they’re so pretty!”

“So, leave them,” Dr. Tallamy advocates. But ALSO plant other hydrangeas that are beneficial.

What’s a little crazy is the fact that these beneficials are actually gorgeous! You can easily distinguish them by their open lace-cap blooms - thousands of tiny, fuzzy fertile flowers that pollinators love. In nature, the giant showy outer petals are just billboards designed to catch a pollinator’s eye. The real magic happens in the middle, where the tiny fertile buds provide a rich feast of pollen and nectar.

When we buy heavily altered non-native imports or mutated “snowball” cultivars, those vital fertile flowers are completely bred out or buried so deeply that insects can’t reach them. If you really want to promote a healthy mountain ecosystem without sacrificing beauty, look for these specific, high-utility varieties.

The Best Native Smooth Hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens)

Our native smooth hydrangea is a powerhouse on shaded mountain slopes. While the mutated Annabelle variety is a wildlife dead-end, several exceptional cultivars keep the open structure that insects need.

  • Haas Halo: Think Haas Halo first. This native selection is an absolute champion. In extensive multi-year trials conducted by the Mt. Cuba Center, Haas Halo outperformed almost every other smooth hydrangea on the market. It features massive, 14-inch lace-cap blooms on sturdy, deep green stems that native bees absolutely swarm.
  • Invincibelle Lace: Think Invincibelle Lace if you want color. This selection provides gorgeous, plum-purple lace-cap flowers on ruby-red stems, offering a striking visual punch while remaining highly attractive to bees.
  • Total Eclipse and Mary Nell: These lesser-known native cultivars also scored top marks for pollinator traffic in scientific evaluations. They are packed with exposed, fertile flowers and serve as crucial larval host plants for local moths, including the spectacular hydrangea sphinx moth, which I didn’t even know was a thing.

The Best Native Oakleaf Hydrangeas (Hydrangea quercifolia)

Native to the woodland edges of the Southeastern United States, oakleaf hydrangeas are tough, require very little maintenance, and handle our local soils beautifully.

  • Alice: Think Alice for grand scale. This robust selection grows up to 12 feet tall and produces colossal, open white flower spikes that age to a stunning dusty pink.
  • Pee Wee: Think Pee Wee for smaller spaces. This compact, dwarf oakleaf option retains the single-flower accessibility of the wild species but fits perfectly into standard foundation plantings or smaller backyard borders.
  • Ruby Slippers and Snow Queen: Both of these popular cultivars keep their open, single-flowered shapes. They remain highly accessible to foraging bees while putting on an incredible autumn foliage show, with leaves that turn brilliant shades of deep crimson and burgundy.

Unique Regional Gems

If you want to introduce your neighbors to something truly unique, look for the Ashy or Silver-Leaf Hydrangea (Hydrangea radiata). This species is native right here to a small handful of counties in the southern Appalachian Mountains. It features flat, creamy-white lace-cap blooms, but its best attribute is the foliage. The undersides of the dark green leaves are a bright, clean silver-white. When breezes catch the canopy, the entire shrub appears to shimmer.

Even if you can't resist a few non-natives, you can still find pollinator allies. Think of the not-so-native Quick Fire (Hydrangea paniculata), which is a pollinator magnet with its open, loose lace-cap structure that blooms pretty early.

By trading high-maintenance turf or sterile imports for these thriving, open-flowered varieties, you can have a gorgeous yard that actively feeds our native bees, butterflies, and birds.

SIDEBAR: Your Garden Center Cheat Sheet

Before you head out to local treasures like the Reflection Riding Native Plant Nursery right at the base of the mountain, clip out these quick rules of thumb:

  • Avoid the “Double” Blooms: If a plant tag says “double-flowered,” skip it. Those extra layers of decorative petals physically block small insects from getting to the center of the bloom.
  • Look for the Lace Cap: Visually check the flower head. You want a central plate that looks like a cluster of tiny, unopened beads surrounded by a delicate ring of larger petals.
  • Plant at the Drip Line: Hydrangeas love morning sun and afternoon shade. They are the perfect anchor plants for the edges of “soft landing” zones right beneath the shade of your mature canopy trees.
  • Hold the Fertilizer: When planting a new shrub in November, do not add heavy nitrogen fertilizers. You want the plant to focus entirely on its root network, not on pushing out tender new green leaves that will get immediately zapped by our first winter freeze.

Dr. Douglas Tallamy

The principles in this column are based on the work of Dr. Douglas Tallamy, the T. A. Baker Professor of Agriculture at the University of Delaware and co-founder of Homegrown National Park. A recipient of the prestigious George Robert White Medal of Honor, his research proves that the choices we make in our home gardens can save local biodiversity.

* * *

Ferris Robinson is the author of three children’s books, “The Queen Who Banished Bugs,” “The Queen Who Accidentally Banished Birds,” and “Call Me Arthropod” in her pollinator series “If Bugs Are Banished.” “Making Arrangements” is her first novel and is available in paperback and on Kindle. “Dogs and Love - Stories of Fidelity” is a collection of true tales about man’s best friend. She is the editor of The Lookout Mountain Mirror and The Signal Mountain Mirror and a Doug Tallamy groupie.
